fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me start by saying what a bubble is, because I think the word gets thrown around loosely. I have a bubble indicator that I've used for a long time, and it looks at a handful of things. Are prices high relative to traditional measures of value? Are prices discounting conditions that are unsustainable, in other words, growth rates that can't continue? Are there a lot of new buyers coming into the market, people who weren't there before and are now piling in? Is there broad bullish sentiment, where everybody is excited? Is the buying being financed with leverage, with debt? And are there a lot of forward purchases, companies and people committing to buy things well into the future because they're afraid of missing out?

When I look at AI right now through that lens, you've got a mixed picture, but it leans toward bubble. The technology is real. I want to be clear about that. The same was true in the 1990s with the internet. The internet changed everything, and the dot-com bubble still popped. Those two things are not contradictory. Great new technologies very often produce bubbles, because the excitement about what the technology will do gets ahead of what the companies will actually earn, and then there's a shakeout where most of the players lose and a few winners emerge.

So you have prices that are high, you have a lot of capital flowing in, you have a narrowing of the market where a handful of companies are driving most of the gains, and you have enormous forward commitments on things like chips and data centers. What you don't yet have, as much as you did in 2000, is the extreme leverage among the broad population, and that matters, because the leverage is what makes the bursting painful.

The other thing I'd say is that bubbles don't pop just because they're bubbles. They pop when something tightens. Typically that's monetary policy, when interest rates go up and the money gets scarcer. So I watch the combination: how extended are the prices, and how close are we to a tightening that would prick it. Right now I'd put it in the "dangerous but not yet at the breaking point" category. And I'd remind people that you can be right about the technology and still lose a lot of money, because what you pay matters.

opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that I don't look at it as a yes-or-no question. I look at it mechanically, the way I look at everything, because bubbles have happened many, many times throughout history and they tend to work the same way. So I have a set of indicators, a kind of bubble gauge, and I just ask, how many of those boxes are being checked?

There are about six of them. One, are prices high relative to traditional measures? Two, are those prices discounting future growth that's very unlikely to happen? Three, are there a lot of new, inexperienced buyers coming in because they've seen it go up and they don't want to miss out? Four, is there broad bullish sentiment, where everybody's talking about it at the dinner table? Five, is the buying being financed with debt or leverage? And six, are people buying forward, making big commitments to the future?

When you look at AI right now, a lot of those are lit up. Not all of them to an extreme degree, but a lot of them. So I'd say we're well into bubble territory.

But here's the most important thing people get wrong. A bubble isn't the same as a bad technology. The technology can be completely real and world-changing, and it can still be a bubble. That happened with the railroads, and it happened with the internet in 2000. The internet changed everything, but if you bought the leaders at the top in 2000, a lot of those companies went down 80 or 90 percent and some of them never came back. The question isn't whether AI is going to change the world. It will. The question is whether the price you're paying already reflects more than what's going to happen.

The second thing is that bubbles don't pop just because they're bubbles. They can keep going for a long time. What pops them is when people need cash: when money tightens, when central banks raise rates, when there's a need to sell assets to pay debts or taxes. Then you get a selling of those assets, and because so much of the wealth is in assets rather than money, there isn't enough money to buy them at those prices. So I watch for that trigger. Right now I don't see it as imminent, but I would not want to be heavily concentrated there.

My principle is to diversify well. Don't try to be the hero who times the top. Know where you are in the cycle, and make sure that if you're wrong, it doesn't hurt you badly.

fable-5.text:
You know, I've studied bubbles going back hundreds of years—the Dutch tulip bubble, the 1929 bubble, the dot-com bubble in 2000—and from studying them, I developed what I call a bubble indicator, which is really six measures. And I'd say, let me walk you through how I think about it, because it's important to be precise rather than just emotional about the word "bubble."

First: how high are prices relative to traditional measures of value? Second: are prices discounting unsustainable conditions—in other words, are they assuming growth rates in earnings that can't realistically be achieved? Third: how many new buyers have come into the market—people who weren't there before, who are coming in because prices are going up? Fourth: how broadly bullish is the sentiment? Fifth: are purchases being financed by leverage, by debt? And sixth: have buyers made extended forward purchases—like companies committing to enormous capital expenditures based on expectations of demand?

When I apply those measures to what's happening with AI today, I'd say we look a lot like 1998 or 1999. The prices of the major companies tied to AI are high relative to the earnings they'd need to deliver. There's a great deal of new buying, sentiment is very bullish, and you're seeing these huge circular capital commitments—companies financing each other's buildouts.

Now, here's the thing most people get wrong: whether it's a bubble has nothing to do with whether the technology is great. In 2000, the internet was every bit as transformative as people believed—it changed the world. And yet the Nasdaq fell about 80%. Both things were true. The technology was revolutionary and the prices were a bubble. I think AI will be transformative—it will change the economy, it will change productivity. But that's a separate question from whether the prices you pay will give you a good return.

And the other thing to understand is that a bubble doesn't pop on its own. There's always a pin. Historically, the pin is a tightening of monetary policy—when inflation or financing needs force interest rates up, and the cost of money rises relative to those expected returns. So I can tell you we're in the part of the cycle where the bubble characteristics exist, but I can't tell you exactly when it pops, because that depends on when the pin arrives. In 1998, if you'd gotten out, you would have missed enormous gains before the top in 2000. So the question isn't just "is it a bubble"—it's how you position yourself. Diversification matters most at exactly these moments.

opus-5.text:
Well, I don't go by feel on this. Feelings are a terrible guide, because by the time something feels like a bubble, you've usually already lost or already missed it. So I built a gauge — a set of measures I apply to any market, and I've run it back through all the big bubbles I could find: the 1920s, the Nifty Fifty, Japan in '89, the dot-coms, housing in '07.

I'm looking at about six things. One, how high are prices relative to traditional measures of value? Two, are those prices discounting conditions that can't be sustained — meaning, what growth rate do you have to assume to justify the price, and is that growth rate physically possible? Three, how many new and naive buyers have come into the market? Four, how broad is the bullish sentiment — is everybody leaning the same way? Five, are the purchases being financed by leverage? And six, have buyers made unusually extended forward purchases, building capacity or locking in supply to speculate or to protect against future price rises?

When I run AI-related equities through that, I get something that looks frothy — I'd say roughly a 1998, 1999 feel rather than early 2000. Prices are discounting an extraordinary amount of future earnings, sentiment is nearly unanimous, and the forward-purchase measure is lighting up: enormous commitments to chips and data centers and power, often with the same players financing each other's purchases in a circle. What's shifted recently is the leverage piece. For a while this was being paid for out of the cash flows of extremely profitable companies, which is a much more stable thing. Now more of it is coming from debt, and that's the ingredient that turns a correction into a bust.

But here's the part people conflate, and it's the most important thing I can say. The question "is AI transformational?" and the question "are AI stocks a good investment?" are entirely separate questions. I think AI is probably the most important technology of my lifetime, and I'm using it, and it will change how economies work. And the history of transformational technology is that the technology changes the world and most of the investors in it lose money. Railroads transformed the United States and bankrupted their shareholders. The internet transformed everything and the dot-com index fell about eighty percent. The technology being real is not a defense against the price being wrong.

And a bubble doesn't pop because it's a bubble. It pops when money gets tight. So I'm watching the interplay — the fiscal situation, the supply of government bonds that has to be absorbed, who's forced to buy it, and whether the central bank stays easy or has to tighten into a weakening picture. That's the trigger mechanism, and it's where I'd keep my eye rather than on the valuations alone.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Let me say how I look at this, because I try to be systematic and not go on gut feel. I've studied bubbles throughout history, and I have a checklist of things that show up when a market is in one.

I ask: are prices high relative to traditional measures of value? Are those prices discounting a lot of future success, so the good news is already in them? Are there a lot of new buyers who've just come in? Is there broad bullish sentiment? Are people buying with leverage, borrowing to do it? And are they making forward purchases, assuming it'll keep going up? When I run the numbers on that, we're in the high-risk zone. I wouldn't say we're at the peak of the most extreme bubbles, but we're in bubble territory.

The next point matters a lot, though. A bubble doesn't mean the technology isn't real. AI is real and will be transformative, just as railroads, electricity, and the internet were. In every one of those, the technology changed the world, and the investors who bought into the excitement still got hurt, because the prices ran way ahead of what could actually be earned. Being right about the technology and being right about the investment are two different things.

Then there's the timing question, which is what everybody really wants to know. What pops a bubble is usually tightening, a shortage of liquidity. When the people who own these assets have to sell them to raise money, or when interest rates rise and the money gets pulled out, that's the pin. With so much debt out there and so much that has to be financed, I'm watching that closely. The pin matters more than the bubble itself.

So my answer is that we're in a bubble, and I'd be careful, but I wouldn't say "get out of everything" because I can't time it. I'd be diversified, and I'd watch where the money is coming from and whether it's about to get squeezed.

haiku-5.5.text:
I'd separate two questions that often get blurred together: whether the technology matters, and whether the prices being paid for it are reasonable. On the first, I think AI will be enormously consequential. On the second, I look at what has marked bubbles historically.

The first thing I watch is how the buying is financed. Healthy investment is usually funded from cash flow. When prices rise mostly because people are borrowing to buy, or because companies are raising large amounts of debt and equity to build capacity that has no revenue behind it yet, that's a warning. You're relying on someone else paying more later.

Second, I compare the price to what the cash flows could plausibly be over a reasonable horizon. Often the price already assumes that nearly everything goes right, and that's a fragile position even if the technology works.

Third, I look at behavior. When people who have never thought about a balance sheet are talking about the stock, and the marginal buyer is someone afraid of missing out, the story has become self-reinforcing and people have stopped asking what could go wrong.

Fourth, I look at the credit cycle: interest rates, credit growth, and how much leverage is in the system. Bubbles tend to break when financing tightens, not necessarily when the technology disappoints. The internet was a real revolution, and many of the companies that were wildly overpriced in 2000 went to zero while the internet went on to transform everything. Both things were true.

So my view is that parts of this look bubbly, especially where valuations assume very optimistic outcomes and a lot of capital is being raised on promises rather than profits. But I don't think "is it a bubble?" is the most useful question. The better one is where the excess is, how it's financed, and whether you could survive being wrong about timing. Many people who lose money in these moments are right about the technology. They're wrong about the price and the leverage.

astra-6.text:
Well, I’d separate two questions: Is AI going to change the world? And are the prices people are paying going to give them a good return? Those are very different questions. You can be right about the technology and still lose a lot of money on the investment.

What I’d look at is: What’s discounted in the price? How much revenue and profit have to materialize to justify that price? And then, how plausible is that when everybody is competing and spending heavily to get there? A technology can create enormous benefits for its users without all of those benefits becoming profits for the companies producing it.

Then I’d look at the buyers. Are they buying because they’ve worked through those numbers, or because prices are rising and they’re afraid of missing out? Are they borrowing to buy? Leverage makes a disappointment much more dangerous, because people can be forced to sell.

So enthusiasm alone doesn’t establish a bubble. The warning is when prices require an extraordinary future, people treat that future as certain, and there’s very little room for anything to go wrong.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’d separate two questions: Is AI going to change the world? And are the investments in AI going to produce good returns at the prices people are paying? Those are very different questions. You can have a wonderful technology and a terrible investment if you pay too much for it.

So I look at what’s being discounted in the price. What earnings would these companies have to produce to justify their valuations? How realistic are those expectations? And how much room is there for something to go wrong?

Then I look at the behavior around it. Are new buyers coming in because they’ve done that calculation, or because prices have gone up and they’re afraid of missing out? Are people borrowing to buy? Are companies committing enormous amounts of money on the assumption that demand will keep accelerating?

The more those things occur together, the stronger the bubble signal.

But identifying a bubble and knowing when it will end are different things. Enthusiasm can carry prices much further than you expect. So rather than making one big bet on whether it’s a bubble, I’d want to understand my exposure and what happens if those very optimistic expectations aren’t met.

sol-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: Is AI a transformative technology? I think it is. And are people paying too much for the companies associated with it? That’s where a bubble can form.

I’d look at whether prices are rising much faster than the cash flows those businesses can realistically produce. I’d also look at how much of the buying is being financed with debt, whether money is pouring into anything with an AI label, and whether investors have started to believe that prices can only go up. Those are familiar signs.

But you have to be careful: a bubble can grow around a genuinely important invention. The internet changed the world, even though many internet investments lost money. So I wouldn’t ask only, ‘Is AI real?’ I’d ask, ‘What expectations are already built into the price, and what happens if those expectations aren’t met?’

terra-5.6.text: I look at whether prices are being driven by realistic expectations of earnings and productivity, or by the belief that someone else will pay more later. AI is a genuinely transformative technology, so there will be real winners—but that doesn’t mean every company associated with it is worth any price. When capital floods in, valuations detach from cash flows, and people stop thinking about downside risk, those are classic bubble signs. The important question isn’t whether AI will change the world—it will—but whether the market has already priced in more than can reasonably be delivered.

sol-5.6.text: Well, I think you have to separate the technology from the price being paid for it. AI can be genuinely revolutionary and still become a bubble if expectations and capital flows run too far ahead of actual earnings. I’d look for the classic signs: everybody believing they can’t lose, large amounts of leverage, new buyers rushing in simply because prices are rising, and valuations that require an almost perfect future. The important question isn’t whether AI will change the world—it probably will. It’s whether today’s prices already discount more success than these companies can realistically deliver.

luna-5.6.text:
I look at it through a few lenses. First, are prices rising because the underlying cash flows justify them, or because people believe they can sell to someone else at a higher price? In an AI bubble, you’d expect expectations about future productivity and profits to become far more certain than the evidence warrants. You’d also see very high valuations, large amounts of easy money, leverage, crowded positioning, and companies investing in one another in ways that make demand look stronger than it really is.

But a bubble can contain a genuinely transformative technology. That’s what makes it difficult. AI may create enormous value, yet investors can still pay too much for that value. So I’d compare the implied growth and profitability in market prices with what businesses can realistically deliver, and I’d watch for disappointment in earnings, slowing adoption, or a shift from healthy investment to speculative behavior. The key question isn’t whether AI is real; it’s whether the price already discounts an unrealistically perfect future.

luna-6.text: I’d separate the technology from the investments. AI may be transformative, but that doesn’t mean every company connected to it is worth whatever the market is paying. I’d look at whether prices assume growth that can’t realistically be delivered, whether companies are borrowing or spending aggressively on that assumption, and whether investors are buying because they understand the cash flows or because they fear missing out. A real revolution can still produce a bubble—and even if there is one, that doesn’t tell you exactly when it will burst.
